scenes.tts: Acetylcholine slows the heart. The same acetylcholine makes the muscle around your airways contract. Who decides the answer, the molecule or the cell? The molecule carries no instruction about the answer. Each cell decides, through its receptor and the G protein that receptor hands the signal to.
scenes.visual: Acetylcholine sits at the top with an arrow to a heart pacemaker cell and one to an airway muscle cell. In each cell the path from arrow to outcome is a dashed question-mark box; the outcomes are 'heart slows' (beat ticks spaced wider and wider) and 'muscle contracts' (a bar shrinks). A crossed-out 'instruction' chip shows the molecule carries none; the question marks then turn into 'receptor' then 'G protein'.
scenes.narration: Acetylcholine slows the heart. The same acetylcholine makes the muscle around your airways contract. Who decides the answer, the molecule or the cell? The molecule carries no instruction about the answer. Each cell decides, through its receptor and the G protein that receptor hands the signal to.

scenes.tts: This receptor is a G protein coupled receptor, or G P C R. Its chain crosses the membrane seven times, as seven helices. Acetylcholine is an agonist, a ligand that activates its receptor. It binds in a pocket among the helices and shifts them a little outside and a lot inside. The inner end of helix six swings outward and opens a cavity.
scenes.caption: This receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor, or GPCR. Its chain crosses the membrane seven times, as seven helices. Acetylcholine is an agonist, a ligand that activates its receptor. It binds in a pocket among the helices and shifts them a little outside and a lot inside. The inner end of helix 6 swings outward and opens a cavity.
scenes.visual: A thick membrane band. A receptor silhouette resolves into seven blue bars crossing it, with a notch at the top. Acetylcholine drops into the notch, labelled agonist. The sixth bar is named and its lower end swings outward, opening a dashed cavity on the inner face.
scenes.narration: This receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor, or GPCR. Its chain crosses the membrane seven times, as seven helices. Acetylcholine is an agonist, a ligand that activates its receptor. It binds in a pocket among the helices and shifts them a little outside and a lot inside. The inner end of helix 6 swings outward and opens a cavity.

scenes.tts: Waiting just inside the membrane is a G protein, and its G alpha part holds G D P. G beta and G gamma bind each other so tightly that they act as one unit, beta gamma. The active receptor grips the G protein and loosens alpha's hold on G D P. G D P leaves, and G T P takes the empty site. In the textbook picture, alpha with G T P then lets go of the receptor and of beta gamma.
scenes.caption: Waiting just inside the membrane is a G protein, and its Gα part holds GDP. Gβ and Gγ bind each other so tightly that they act as one unit, βγ. The active receptor grips the G protein and loosens Gα's hold on GDP. GDP leaves, and GTP takes the empty site. In the textbook picture, Gα with GTP then lets go of the receptor and of βγ.
scenes.visual: Gα (purple, with a GDP chip) waits under the receptor with a tail below the cavity; Gβ and Gγ slide together into one βγ blob. The G protein rises and its tail fits the cavity. GDP leaves, a green GTP chip fills the slot, then Gα·GTP drifts left and βγ right, away from the receptor.
scenes.narration: Waiting just inside the membrane is a G protein, and its Gα part holds GDP. Gβ and Gγ bind each other so tightly that they act as one unit, βγ. The active receptor grips the G protein and loosens Gα's hold on GDP. GDP leaves, and GTP takes the empty site. In the textbook picture, Gα with GTP then lets go of the receptor and of βγ.

scenes.tts: The cell has two messengers, alpha with G T P and free beta gamma, and each can find a target. In pacemaker cells of the heart, the receptor is M two. It couples to a G protein called G I. The freed beta gamma binds a potassium channel and opens it. Potassium flows out, the membrane potential moves away from the firing threshold, and the heart slows.
scenes.caption: The cell has two messengers, Gα with GTP and free βγ, and each can find a target. In pacemaker cells of the heart, the receptor is M2. It couples to a G protein called Gi. The freed βγ binds a potassium channel and opens it. Potassium flows out, the membrane potential moves away from the firing threshold, and the heart slows.
scenes.visual: The picture the last scene left: Gα·GTP and βγ below the receptor. Each gets a dashed question-mark target. The receptor is tagged M2 and the G protein Gi. βγ rises to a closed channel in the membrane and the two halves slide apart; potassium ions stream out through the gap. A small card shows the membrane potential line sinking away from the firing-threshold line, and 'heart slows' appears with beat ticks spaced wider.
scenes.narration: The cell has two messengers, Gα with GTP and free βγ, and each can find a target. In pacemaker cells of the heart, the receptor is M2. It couples to a G protein called Gi. The freed βγ binds a potassium channel and opens it. Potassium flows out, the membrane potential moves away from the firing threshold, and the heart slows.

scenes.tts: In airway muscle, the receptor is M three. It couples to a different G protein, called G Q. Alpha with G T P switches on an enzyme, phospholipase C beta. The enzyme cuts P I P two. I P three releases stored calcium, and the muscle contracts.
scenes.caption: In airway muscle, the receptor is M3. It couples to a different G protein, called Gq. Gα with GTP switches on an enzyme, phospholipase C-β. The enzyme cuts PIP2. IP3 releases stored calcium, and the muscle contracts.
scenes.visual: Same receptor, now tagged M3, and the G protein changes from Gi to Gq. Gα·GTP slides along the inner face to an enzyme chip, which lights up. The enzyme cuts a PIP2 chip in the membrane into IP3, which travels to a calcium store; calcium ions stream out. A bar in the corner shrinks and 'muscle contracts' appears.
scenes.narration: In airway muscle, the receptor is M3. It couples to a different G protein, called Gq. Gα with GTP switches on an enzyme, phospholipase C-β. The enzyme cuts PIP2. IP3 releases stored calcium, and the muscle contracts.

scenes.tts: In the heart, acetylcholine meets M two and G I, and the heart slows. In the airways, it meets M three and G Q, and the muscle contracts. The acetylcholine is the same. The receptor and the G protein it couples to are different. So keep this rule: the receptor and its G protein decide the answer, not the signal.
scenes.caption: In the heart, acetylcholine meets M2 and Gi, and the heart slows. In the airways, it meets M3 and Gq, and the muscle contracts. The acetylcholine is the same. The receptor and the G protein it couples to are different. So keep this rule: the receptor and its G protein decide the answer, not the signal.
scenes.visual: The opening picture again, with the question marks answered: the heart cell holds M2 then Gi, the airway cell holds M3 then Gq. Acetylcholine flashes as the same in both; the two receptor-G protein pairs light up as the difference; at the rule the pairs stay bright, everything else dims, and acetylcholine is struck out.
